observation.visible_scene: Two three‑lobed fidget spinners with anodized rainbow‑colored bodies and a gold/brass central bearing cap rest on a flat, uniform light‑gray surface. One spinner sits in the upper‑left background (slightly out of focus), the other in the lower‑right foreground (in focus). Both are spinning in place about their central axes for the whole excerpt; the central gold caps stay fixed while the three lobes turn, and the lobes show motion blur and shifting color reflections (green, blue, purple, yellow) as they rotate. The spinner centers do not translate across the frame, indicating object rotation rather than camera movement.
visible_changes: Both spinners rotate continuously throughout the segment, evidenced by the changing angular orientation of their three lobes from frame to frame.
Persistent motion blur on the lobes of both spinners indicates sustained rotational speed (not a still pose).
The iridescent color patches on each lobe shift position and hue as the surfaces turn relative to the light, producing reflections that move with the lobes.
The background spinner (upper left) rotates in the same manner as the foreground one; its lobes reorient across the frames while its gold hub remains centered.
No change in the position of either spinner's center on the surface, and the gray background plane stays fixed, so the visible change is rotation of the objects, not translation or camera pan.
outside_clip_unknowns: How the spinners were set spinning (no hand, push, or onset is shown within the excerpt).
Whether the rotation continues, slows, or stops after the last frame, or what preceded the first frame.
The exact spin direction and angular speed of each spinner, which cannot be reliably measured from these sparse samples.
uncertain_details: The precise rotation direction (clockwise vs. counter‑clockwise) of each spinner is not clearly determinable from the sampled frames.
Whether the two spinners rotate at the same rate or in the same direction is uncertain.

Minor apparent shifts in framing could be tiny camera movement or simply the rotation of the objects; the background gives insufficient evidence to confirm any camera motion, so the scene is treated as a static camera with rotating objects.
